Why use dynamic routing instead of static routes?
Static routes don't scale and don't react to failures. With dynamic routing, routers share what they know, fill in each other's tables, and reroute when something changes.
What two things does a network statement under router eigrp do?

1. Turns EIGRP on for every interface whose IP falls in that range: it sends hellos there and listens for neighbors.
2. Includes those interfaces' networks in what it advertises.
What does EIGRP need for two routers to become neighbors?
EIGRP enabled on both interfaces (matching network statements), the same AS number, and both interfaces in the same subnet.
R1 and R2 share 192.168.2.0/24. R1 has network 192.168.1.0 and network 192.168.2.0. R2 has only network 192.168.3.0. Both use router eigrp 1. Do they become neighbors?
No. R2 isn't running EIGRP on the shared link, so it neither sends hellos there nor listens to R1's.
R1 runs router eigrp 1 and R2 runs router eigrp 10, with network statements covering the shared link. Do they become neighbors?
No. The AS numbers have to match.
R1 (10.0.0.1/30) and R2 (10.0.0.6/30) are cabled together and both run router eigrp 50 with network 10.0.0.0. Neighbors?
No. They're in different /30s (0-3 and 4-7), so they aren't on the same subnet.
You enter network 172.16.5.0 under router eigrp 1 with no wildcard. Which interfaces does it match?
Every interface in 172.16.0.0/16. With no wildcard, EIGRP uses the classful size (172.16 is class B, so /16), and the config shows network 172.16.0.0.
network 10.0.0.0 with no wildcard: what's the risk?
It matches every interface in 10.0.0.0/8 (classful class A). Any interface you didn't intend that's in 10.x gets EIGRP too.
network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.127. Does it enable EIGRP on an interface at 192.168.1.10/24? What subnet gets advertised?
Yes, 192.168.1.10 falls inside 192.168.1.0-127. It advertises 192.168.1.0/24, the interface's own subnet. The statement only picks interfaces.
network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.127. Does it enable EIGRP on an interface at 192.168.1.200/25?
Gi0/0 is 192.168.1.1/25 and Gi0/1 is 192.168.1.129/25. You enter network 192.168.1.0 with no wildcard. What's enabled and advertised?
Both interfaces (both fall in classful 192.168.1.0/24). It advertises two routes: 192.168.1.0/25 and 192.168.1.128/25.
What does passive-interface do under a routing protocol?
Stops hellos on that interface, so no neighbors form there, but its network is still advertised. Used on LAN-facing and ISP-facing interfaces.
Why not enable EIGRP on the ISP-facing interface?
You'd be offering your internal routes to the outside and trying to form neighbors where none should exist. Only enable it where your own routers should peer.
Are routing protocol hellos replies to each other?

No. Each router sends hellos on a timer whether or not anyone's listening. A neighbor forms when each hears the other. (OSPF hellos list the neighbors heard, which confirms the conversation goes both ways.)
After router eigrp 1 and the first network statement, show ip route shows nothing new. Why?
No neighbor yet. Routes only arrive once another router on a shared link runs EIGRP too and the two form a neighbor relationship.
What's the routing table code and default AD for an internal EIGRP route?
D, AD 90.
What metric does each use: RIP, OSPF, EIGRP, BGP?

RIP: hop count.
OSPF: cost, from interface bandwidth.
EIGRP: a formula built from bandwidth and delay.
BGP: a list of path attributes checked in order.
Two OSPF paths lead to a network. An engineer lowers the bandwidth value on one path's interface. What happens?
That interface's OSPF cost goes up, so OSPF prefers the other path. The real link speed doesn't change.
Two OSPF routers on a shared link see each other but get stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE. Most likely cause?
An MTU mismatch between the two interfaces.
A link two hops away fails. What happens to a static route through it, versus an EIGRP route?

Static: stays installed and keeps sending traffic into the failure.
EIGRP: learns about the failure and removes the route, or switches to another path if one exists.
Which routing protocol do you configure on the CCNA, and which one runs between ISPs?
OSPF on the CCNA. BGP between ISPs and organizations on the internet.
Why is BGP deliberately slow to react?
The internet has a huge number of networks going up and down all the time. If every change rippled out instantly, routers everywhere would be overwhelmed. BGP trades speed for stability.
